title: Jensen Huang and Silicon Valley’s Short-Term Thinking
text:
Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts 

 Just like that, Jensen Huang is back on top. Reportedly, President Trump called Nvidia’s board and encouraged it to reinstate the former CEO, who had been pushed out only two weeks earlier. The board made the “correct and proper decision,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, which ensures the “Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy.” The president seemed happy. Tech leaders were relieved. The stock market seemed to rally with the news. A lot of other interested parties, however, still have burning questions.

 Lawmakers from both parties are planning to grill Huang about the affair he had with a suspected Chinese spy and the related threats to national security. But how will Americans, who just voted resoundingly against AI, data centers, and grift among the rich, receive the president giving a pass to his tech-CEO friend? On this episode of Radio Atlantic , Charlie Warzel talks about Nvidia, Huang, the short-term thinking of tech CEOs, and an economy held hostage by AI.

 The following is a transcript of the episode: 

 Charlie Warzel: We just had an election where, as you alluded to, America expressed deep concern with artificial intelligence in general, with data centers, which are the thing that house all the Nvidia chips. And you have a class of new lawmakers who are coming in with a mandate from America to try to rein in this, like, tech-elite class, this AI economy that people feel is akin to a hostage situation, right? You’re gonna have, like, all of that collide in D.C., and I think it’s gonna be a nightmare. I really do.

 [ Music ] 

 Hanna Rosin: Today, Jensen Huang was reinstated as chairman of Nvidia, the chip-manufacturing giant. Elon Musk posted on X, “The mistake has been corrected.” The president referred to it as the “correct and proper decision” and posted an AI-generated meme showing Huang in the same raised-fist pose that Trump himself adopted after the 2024 assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania.

 So for the president, for Huang, and for other tech giants: order restored. For a lot of other people, though—what?

 I’m Hanna Rosin. This is Radio Atlantic .

 It’s been just about two weeks since Huang, who is close to the president, admitted to having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. Congressional leaders are at this very moment continuing to call up Huang to testify about the dangers his affair posed to national security.

 The showdown with China over spying, over AI dominance, is still a looming threat of our era. And yet, there is Huang, right back in his corner office with his latest leather jacket.

 Joining me to discuss is tech writer and host of the Galaxy Brain podcast Charlie Warzel.

 Charlie, we are here once again talking about the story that never stops giving. Welcome to the show.

 Warzel: Thank you for having me. I told you this is the nightmare scenario two weeks ago, and here we are in the nightmare.

 Rosin: I knew that was my first question. So when you woke up this morning to the news that Huang was reinstated at Nvidia, do you think, No way ? Or I knew this was gonna happen. I told you so ?

 Warzel: Somewhere in between, honestly. It was starting to get—on Sunday, [Treasury Secretary] Scott Bessent sort of walked back a little bit. He was on—I believe on CBS—one of the morning shows, and he initially took this very strident position that the Nvidia board needed to look outside the company for leadership. And then when pressed on it again, he kind of backtracked and said, Well, you know, Jensen Huang is actually now on the outside . And so that signaled a little to me that this week could get a little crazy. I didn’t anticipate it happening this quickly, though.

 Rosin: I mean, there has been a lot of reporting that President Trump was involved in the decision, that he called into the Nvidia board meeting to advocate for the return of Huang. What do we know so far about the president’s involvement?

 Warzel: I mean, this is—I don’t know if it’s unprecedented. But this is a lot of involvement from the president of the United States in a publicly traded company’s personnel decisions to—he said he both intervened directly and indirectly, whatever indirectly means. But there were calls, supposedly. There have been communications over the recent weeks with Trump and Jensen Huang, who are cellphone buddies. It’s remarkable.

 The hedge-fund manager Bill Ackman said that the wisdom of the crowd has spoken , which I think is a very odd way to describe the president of the United States intervening in the workings of a corporate board. But hey, the wisdom of a crowd has spoken, I guess.

 Rosin: Okay, so what we know so far is that the president was probably heavily involved in the decision to return back to the top of this company someone who was implicated in a national-security scandal. So it’s not obvious why a president would intervene in that way. So let’s unpack it a little bit. One theory why Trump would intervene in this way is the economy, right?

 Warzel: So there’s a lot here. As we talked about on a previous episode of this, as a lot of people, including myself, have written about and reported on: Nvidia, in some ways, can be seen as , like, a load-bearing block of the global economy, right? They both power the AI boom with their chips. They also invest into the AI companies through this, like, five-layer cake that Jensen Huang helped create, the circular financing, right? So they both power the boom; they finance the boom. That makes them very critical to the global economy. There are a lot of people who argue that Jensen Huang essentially, like, is the one man whose fate determines whether the market goes up and down.

 Nvidia stock for a while was down, but the rest of the economy was doing okay. It was kind of shouldering this. And then late last week, there was a pretty big sell-off led by a lot of tech stocks. And a lot of the year’s gains in the S&P 500 were lost. So people were kind of freaking out. I think it’s also no coincidence that this was announced—Huang’s reinstatement came—just, you know, right before the markets opened on Monday, after this huge sell-off on Friday. So the economy is a big part of this. Donald Trump believes, according to all the reporting that we’ve seen, that Jensen Huang is a critical part of the AI boom, which is, you know, propping up the rest of the stock market.

 Rosina: So it’s not just that Nvidia is too big to fail. It too much of a risk. It’s Jensen Wang, specifically?

 Warzel: That’s the belief. I mean, that’s at least what a lot of these tech leaders are saying too. So there’s really, like, three cohorts that have been agitating for this. One is Nvidia shareholders, who, obviously, Jensen Huang has made them tons and tons of money, especially if you’ve been a shareholder for a very long time in the company. But even anyone who got in after the ChatGPT revolution has seen huge gains, a stock split. So they want this guy back because he’s made them a lot of money.

 Then you have the Silicon Valley–elite class. I would argue the Silicon Valley–elite class wants this because they want the AI boom to continue. They have a lot riding on this. All the AI CEOs have a whole bunch of investments of their own that are predicated on all the numbers going up and up and up.

 But also, I think, there’s a cultural reason for this, which is: They do not want to see arguably the greatest visionary, the most irreplaceable CEO in Silicon Valley ousted, because it means that they could be ousted. It means that the CEO is vulnerable, that the visionary founder is vulnerable. I think that’s, like, a very big part of this. This is one of the existential crises that these guys have been going through, because everyone thought that Jensen was too big to fail. The fact that he had to resign after all this pressure and the board didn’t want him back is, I think to them, a very, very scary proposition because it means they can no longer act with impunity. So that was one of the reasons.

 And then I think you have Donald Trump, who wanted the economy to keep going on his watch, and this was the thing, the lever he thought he could pull to make number go up.

 Rosin: So it’s like there’s a Silicon Valley myth of a genius, and Trump has used the word genius recently. And that’s a cultural trope, but it’s also real because it drives the stock market. So it’s kind of a circular logic around this word visionary and genius that you just mentioned.

 Warzel: Yeah, I mean, I think that so much of stock markets, it’s a confidence game. And I don’t mean that in the sense of: It’s a con. I mean, it’s about having confidence in the market, having confidence in the direction of things.

 For so long, we have been talking about the economy as being propped up by AI, and we’ve been talking about AI in America as having all this very peculiar circular financing, about Is this a bubble? Is this not a bubble? And there’s this idea around all of it of extreme precarity, right? That all of this is contingent on a big bet that has been made, both about the technology succeeding but also about all of this different type of financing and all this historic investment actually meaning something and going somewhere.

 You need confidence from all of these investors, from all of these folks. Jensen Huang is somebody who, for this class of people, projected a lot of confidence and instilled a lot of confidence in the direction of where the economy and where the AI boom is going. So with him out of it, there was a lot of uncertainty. We were starting to see that in the markets. This freaked a lot of people out.

 Rosin: Right, and they don’t like uncertainty. Okay, let me run another Trump motivation by you. Lately, Trump has been talking about Alice Huang—the woman who Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair with and who U.S. intelligence officials are suspecting to be a spy—has been sort of diminishing her role.

 He said recently, “Every time you have a Chinese woman that’s good-looking or beautiful, they say she’s a spy.” Now we’ve heard this from the president, not from U.S. intelligence officials. And I was wondering if there’s something in here about Trump minimizing affairs because of his own history, sort of minimizing the importance of this kind of scandal taking down a great leader.

 Warzel: I think it’s not only just Trump; it’s all these folks we’re talking about in Silicon Valley. They’ve all been approaching this scandal not from the geopolitical angle of this, but from the moral-infidelity angle, right? Saying, you know, Everyone has their foibles; everyone is flawed; geniuses can be flawed too. Everyone deserves a second chance . And it’s really not a question about morality.

 There’s obviously, you know, the corporate-HR level of things, which is that there’s been reporting about Huang having affairs with employees in the company, including a direct report. Alice Huang was also a client of Nvidia’s, of Jensen Huang, so there’s an impropriety there. But that’s not the thing that people, that lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are upset about right now. They’re upset about the fact that Alice Huang has this alleged tie to Chinese intelligence, and what, if anything, this did to the larger geopolitical question: whether Megaspeed, this company she worked with, was skirting U.S. chip-export bans, allowing Nvidia chips to get into China or to be used by China in these remote-access data centers; or whether or not Alice Huang was reporting on things that Jensen Huang was doing; whether she had access to any of his devices or anything like that—all of those geopolitical concerns.

 So it’s interesting to watch both Trump and all these executives sort of not talk about that, and just focus on this other morality play. But I think what we know is actually very troubling. There’s good evidence to suggest that a lot of chip-smuggling was going on. We don’t know whether Huang and Nvidia were directly related to this, but we know that Megaspeed certainly had some role to play in this ecosystem. And Megaspeed, it should be said, has declined all allegations of wrongdoing here. And The New York Times reported on Sunday that Alice Huang had been keeping in touch with an agent in the Chinese intelligence service for over a year. She’d been speaking with this person and staying in contact with them while she was maintaining this relationship with Jensen Huang. So that’s a lot of time. And it’s very interesting to see that report come out on Sunday and have him get reinstated on Monday.

 [ Music ] 

 Rosin: When we come back, we talk about how this is more than just an economic story.

 [ Break ] 

 Rosin: So right now, at this moment, there are two camps. There’s the President Trump–Jensen Huang tech-leader camp. They want Jensen Huang to come back. But the other track, which is the national-security track, is continuing to move forward. Congressional leaders are still asking Jensen Huang to come and testify. And polls show that Americans actually do care about the national-security risks involved here. So presumably, the story—you and I are gonna be talking about this again. This story is not going to go away.

 Let’s take the congressional testimonies first. What does it look like if you have Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, testifying before Congress with the president’s backing—as opposed to what could have been, which is Jensen Huang, a citizen, not beholden to the company, not the CEO, and without the support of the president?

 Warzel: In an interesting way, this is just a way bigger scandal now. Like, this is a way bigger, thornier, more intense, more interesting scandal. Which, again, if you’re Donald Trump—and, also, people who care about, you know, Nvidia’s relationship to the global economy and the AI boom—the logic doesn’t fully make sense there, right? You would probably want this to go away rather than become, like, the central story of Washington, D.C., for the next 12 months or so. It remains to be seen whether Huang will just come there and plead the Fifth, right? Just say, like, absolutely nothing because basically anything he could say seems like it may or may not jeopardize Nvidia’s position, a bunch of other people. He is now in charge of this company.

 It’s also going to absolutely invigorate the investigations, again, which you’re seeing are coming from both China hawks or just people who are very upset about the way that this has been handled by the Trump administration and Trump’s involvement in getting him reinstated.

 I sort of don’t have words for how charged this is going to be. We just had an election where, as you alluded to, America expressed deep concern with artificial intelligence in general, with data centers, which are the thing that house all the Nvidia chips. And you have a class of new lawmakers who are coming in with a mandate from America to try to rein in this, like, tech-elite class, this AI economy that people feel is akin to a hostage situation, right? You have all of these people saying, If you don’t let us build what we wanna do and act the way that we wanna do, then the numbers gonna go down. All this, you know—the bubble’s gonna pop, and good luck, right? Nice economy you got there; hope nothing happens to it , sort of situation. You’re gonna have, like, all of that collide in D.C., and I think it’s gonna be a nightmare. I really do.

 Rosin: Yeah, that’s absolutely correct because if there is one desire from this midterm flip, it’s accountability. Like, let us enter an era of accountability where rich people don’t get to get away with whatever they want to get away with. That’s what the people seem to be asking for, both in their concerns about corruption, their concerns about data centers, everything that you just mentioned. And this just feels like a sort of pushback to all that.

 Warzel: Absolutely. And I think that a lot of people are gonna have stuff to prove here, right? They’re gonna wanna make an example out of all of this. And I was talking to somebody in Silicon Valley this morning about this, and they were saying to me that the election really showed this really short-term political thinking, right? The tech leaders were so focused on the AI bet that they allowed themselves to get caught up in, you know, hitching their wagon to Trump and the MAGA situation, right? Like, all the donations for the ballroom, the standing behind him at the inauguration, all of the meetings, the fawning, and all of that. And not seeing that the political winds could blow, you know, in other directions, that hitching your star to this guy so completely was a bad calculation. It’s because they had this short-term thinking.

 And this person described this to me as, like, another perfect example of the short-term thinking. Like, yes, we solved this problem in the very near term. The stock market is gonna rally now on all of this. But what’s it gonna mean for this to become a far bigger political scandal? Like, what is that going to mean potentially to, you know, how the Democrats are going to position themselves against AI in 2028? Like, it seems like they are playing checkers instead of, you know, the seven-dimensional chess that they always claim to be playing.

 Rosin: Yeah. Well, Charlie, it looks like there’s gonna be a showdown, and I look forward to talking to you about it when it unfolds. Thank you so much for explaining this to us.

 Warzel: Yeah. Absolutely. Happy to be here.

 Rosin: That is all for today’s show.

 [ Music ] 

 Rosin: This episode of Radio Atlantic was produced by Mike Pesoli and edited by Hadley Robinson. It was engineered by Miguel Carrascal and has original music by Rob Smierciak. Claudine Ebeid is the executive producer of podcasts, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor.

 If you like what you saw here today, new episodes of Radio Atlantic drop every Monday and Thursday. You can find them on The Atlantic ’s YouTube page. You can find them on Apple or Spotify or wherever it is you get your podcasts. And you can subscribe to this publication at TheAtlantic.com/Listener.

 Until next time, I’m Hanna Rosin.
